Owner's Basis of Design - Excerpt
Document OBD-DC2-A, Revision A. Extract of Sections 1, 3, 5 and 9 issued to the design and construction team for the roof structure package.
1  Project identification
3  Facility description
The building is a single-storey, single-occupancy data centre of 240 ft by 180 ft on plan, framed in structural steel, with the top of roof steel at elevation 32 ft-0 in above finished floor and a continuous 3 ft-6 in parapet on all four sides. The facility supports a designated emergency operations tenant and is therefore classified Risk Category III; the Owner requires that the classification be carried through every load case, including the roof snow and lateral cases, and that it not be traded away in value engineering.
A louvred equipment enclosure and a row of packaged rooftop units stand on the main roof within a screened yard. The roof structure runs continuously beneath the enclosure; the enclosure is not a separate roof level.
3.4  Roof framing and roof deck
The roof framing is open-web steel joists at 6 ft-0 in on centre spanning 30 ft-0 in between joist girders on the transverse column lines. The joist girders are supported on the perimeter columns and on the interior column lines.
The roof deck is to be 1.5 in wide-rib (Type B) steel deck of 3 ft-0 in cover width, spanning across the joists in continuous lengths of not less than three spans wherever the framing allows. The deck serves three functions at once - it carries the roof gravity load to the joists, it acts as the roof diaphragm delivering wind and seismic force to the braced frames, and it is the substrate for the roofing assembly - and the Owner expects a single deck package to satisfy all three.
Deck gage, support attachment and sidelap connection are to be developed by the structural engineer of record and are to be shown on the roof deck drawing as zones, so that the erector can set out the work without reference to a calculation package.
5  Programme and procurement
The roof structure package is on the critical path. The Owner's procurement strategy assumes that roof-deck material is on site and available to the erector within 9 weeks of release for fabrication. A deck product, gage or finish that cannot meet that allowance is not available to this project, whatever its structural merit, and the design is to be developed accordingly.
Release for fabrication of the roof deck package: on approval of the roof deck drawing and the deck attachment schedule.
Material on site: not later than 9 weeks after that release.
Substitutions that lengthen the delivery are to be raised with the Owner before they are carried into the design, not after.
9  Design exclusions and agreements with the authority having jurisdiction
The following have been agreed with the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) in the pre-application review and are recorded here so that they are not re-opened:
Thermal effects are excluded from the roof deck design. The roof assembly is fully insulated above the deck and the building is conditioned continuously; the AHJ has agreed that self-straining thermal forces need not be combined with the gravity, snow, wind or seismic effects in the design of the roof deck and its attachments.
The ground snow load for the site is established by a site-specific case study rather than by the mapped value. The study is a separate document and is the only source of the ground snow load for this project.
Roof drainage is by internal drains with secondary overflow scuppers through the parapet; ponding instability is addressed by the drainage design and by the deck stiffness requirements of the structural design criteria.
Nothing in this excerpt relieves the structural engineer of record of the obligation to apply the importance factors and load combinations required for Risk Category III.
Related documents
The structural design criteria for the roof, the site-specific ground snow load case study, the lateral analysis report, the architectural roof plan and the roof structure model develop this basis of design. The current revision of each is listed on the project document transmittal; where a document in the project file carries an earlier revision, the revision listed on the current transmittal governs.

1 Purpose and scope
This report establishes the ground snow load, pg, for the site of the DC-2 Helena Data Centre - Building A in Lewis
and Clark County, Montana. The site lies in an area for which the mapped ground snow load is not given and for
which a site-specific case study is required. The study determines the ground snow load only. It does not determine
roof snow loads, does not select exposure or thermal factors, and does not apply an importance factor; those are
the work of the structural engineer of record and are set out in the structural design criteria for the project.
2 Regulatory basis
The study has been carried out in accordance with the requirements for snow load case studies in the building
code adopted by the authority having jurisdiction, as modified for Department of Defense work by UFC 3-301-01,
Structural Engineering. UFC 3-301-01 paragraph 2-4.5 directs the designer to section 1608.2.3, Snow Load Case
Studies, which requires that, where a case study is made, "the ground snow load is to be determined based on a
Risk Category II structure for this purpose".
2.1 Accordingly, the ground snow load reported in section 6 is determined on a Risk Category II basis. It is a site
characteristic, not a structure-specific design value. The structure served by this study is classified in a higher risk
category; the importance factor appropriate to that classification is applied separately by the structural engineer of
record, in the structural design criteria, and has deliberately not been built into the value reported here. Applying an
importance factor to the value reported in section 6 a second time would be an error.
2.2 Exposure, thermal and slope effects, drift surcharges, rain-on-snow surcharge and the minimum roof snow load
are outside the scope of this study.
3 Site description
The site is a broad bench on the west side of the Missouri River valley at an elevation of 4,880 ft, approximately 4
miles west of Canyon Ferry Reservoir. The bench is open and unobstructed, falling gently to the east. The
surrounding terrain rises steeply to the west into the Continental Divide, where the high-elevation snow course and
SNOTEL network provides a long record of seasonal accumulation. Winter precipitation at the site is orographically
enhanced relative to the valley floor stations to the east and north, and the seasonal snowpack is subject to
repeated mid-winter melt and rain-on-snow episodes that consolidate the pack without removing it.
4 Data sources
Annual maximum ground snow water equivalent has been assembled for seven stations within 30 miles of the site,
spanning an elevation band from 3,830 ft to 7,000 ft. Records were drawn from the National Weather Service
co-operative network, the Natural Resources Conservation Service SNOTEL network and the state climate office
archive. Station records were checked for homogeneity, gaps were flagged rather than filled, and station values

4.1 The annual maximum water equivalent series for the Canyon Ferry Dam station, the closest station to the site,

below the site and its series is not by itself a determination of the ground snow load for the site.
5 Methodology
The study follows the Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory (CRREL) methodology for
site-specific ground snow loads, as used to develop the mapped values in the national standard and as applied in
the published CRREL state and regional snow load studies. The steps are:
5.1 Assemble the annual maximum ground snow water equivalent at each station over its period of record,
converting measured depth to water equivalent where water equivalent was not observed, using the station's own
measured seasonal density where available.
5.2 Fit a log-normal distribution to each station's annual maxima by the method of moments, and extract the
50-year mean recurrence interval value. The log-normal fit is adopted in preference to the Gumbel fit on the
evidence of the probability plots for the valley stations, which show the characteristic upward curvature of a mixed
rain-on-snow population.
5.3 Convert the 50-year water equivalent to a ground snow load in pounds per square foot at 5.20 psf per inch of
water equivalent.
5.4 Regress the station 50-year loads on station elevation over the local elevation band, weighting each station by
its record length, and evaluate the regression at the site elevation. The regression over the seven stations of Table
4-1 gives a coefficient of determination of 0.96 with a standard error of estimate of 6.4 psf.
5.5 Check the regression value against the two nearest long-record stations after adjusting them to the site
elevation individually, and against the state study value for the same elevation band. Adopt the regression value
where the checks agree within the standard error, as they do here.
5.6 The analysis period is the 45 water years 1981 to 2025 for the regression stations with concurrent record,
extended to the full period of record at each station for the distribution fitting of paragraph 5.2. No trend adjustment
has been applied; the Mann-Kendall test on the concurrent period returns no significant trend at the 5 per cent
level.

directed by UFC 3-301-01 paragraph 2-4.5, is:

5.4.2 Surcharge shape. A drift forming against an obstruction of clear height hc = h - hb is triangular, with its peak
at the face of the obstruction and falling linearly to zero at the far edge of the drift. Where hd is not greater than hc
the drift is full height: the peak surcharge is hd x gamma and the drift width is w = 4 hd. Where hd exceeds hc the
drift is truncated by the obstruction: the peak surcharge is hc x gamma and the width is w = min(4 hd^2 / hc, 8 hc).
The surcharge is added to the balanced load pf, and the balanced load acts over the whole roof including beneath
the drift.
5.4.3 Windward face. On the face that the wind arrives at, a windward drift of height 0.75 hd is taken, with lu
equal to the roof fetch from the upwind roof edge to that face.
5.4.4 Sheltered face. On the sheltered face, a leeward drift of height hd is taken, with lu equal to the along-wind
length of the obstruction itself, that is, the dimension of the obstruction measured in the direction the wind is
blowing. The roof of the obstruction is the snow source for that drift.
5.4.5 Wind directions. Wind is considered from each of the four directions in turn. Every obstruction forms a
windward drift on the face the wind arrives at and a leeward drift on its sheltered face in each direction. The design
surcharge at a point on the roof is the largest of the surcharges produced at that point by the four directions; the
four directions are not superimposed.
5.4.6 Parapets. A parapet is treated by the windward rule of clause 5.4.3: the drift height is 0.75 hd with lu equal to
the roof dimension upwind of the parapet, and the clear height is hc = parapet height above the roof surface minus
hb. The parapet on this project is 3 ft-6 in high on all four sides.
5.4.7 Application to the deck. The deck is a local element. Each deck zone must carry the peak surcharge
occurring anywhere within the area it serves, not the average over that area and not the value at its centre.
Where a drift crosses a zone boundary the higher demand governs the whole of the zone it falls in.
5.5 Snow buildup at rooftop obstructions
Per UFC 3-301-01 paragraph 3-4.1, which adopts ASCE 7-22 Section 7.4 [Supplement], snow buildup around
rooftop obstructions is to be considered. Rooftop equipment, equipment curbs, equipment enclosures and screen
walls are obstructions. An obstruction standing more than 2.0 ft above the balanced snow surface (that is, hc
greater than 2.0 ft) is treated as a drift obstruction and is given the full treatment of clause 5.4 on every face.
Shorter obstructions need not be given a drift surcharge, but the balanced load is carried across them.
5.5.1 The equipment enclosure, the equipment screen wall and the packaged rooftop units shown on the current

Prepared by

1 Scope
This report documents the lateral-force-resisting system of the single-storey roof, the roof-level forces the
diaphragm must deliver to it, and the chord and collector members available at the roof level. It is issued so that the
roof deck diaphragm can be designed against a consistent set of roof-level forces and stiffnesses. It does not
design the deck: the deck gage, support attachment and sidelap connection are developed under the structural
design criteria EOR-DC-RD-01.
2 Lateral-force-resisting system
2.1 The lateral-force-resisting system is a set of ordinary concentrically braced frames located in the exterior
walls on all four sides of the building. There are no interior braced bays: the interior of the building is a clear data
hall and the interior columns are gravity columns with pinned connections at the roof. All horizontal force collected
by the roof diaphragm is therefore delivered to the perimeter.
2.2 Each braced frame occupies one 30 ft bay of an exterior wall line and is modelled at the roof level as a discrete
in-plane spring of the stiffness k given in Table 3-1. Frames designated direction X sit in the walls that run in the x
direction and resist force along x; frames designated direction Y sit in the walls that run in the y direction and resist
force along y.
2.3 The roof-level reaction of a frame is delivered at its two column lines, that is, at the two ends of the bay it
occupies, and not as a distributed reaction along the wall. The deck, the perimeter edge member and the collectors
of section 6 must carry the force from the diaphragm to those two points.
2.4 Drag struts extend not less than one bay (30 ft) each side of a braced bay along the wall line.

7 Analysis model and assumptions
7.1 The roof was analysed as a horizontal in-plane assembly at the roof level. The joists, joist girders and the
perimeter edge member were modelled as axial members with the stiffnesses of Table 6-2; the deck panels were
modelled as shear panels between them; the braced frames were modelled as springs of the stiffness k of Table
3-1 acting at the two column lines of each braced bay, in the direction the frame resists.
7.2 The framed roof openings shown on the roof framing plan were modelled as holes in the shear field, with the
opening frames modelled as axial members around them. The shear that would have passed through an opening
redistributes around it and raises the shear in the deck at the opening corners; that increase is a result of the
analysis, not an assumption.
7.3 Out-of-plane stiffness of the roof framing, the stiffness of the roofing assembly and any contribution of the
non-structural screen walls were neglected. Column bases were taken as pinned and the gravity columns were
taken as offering no lateral stiffness.
7.4 The analysis is linear elastic and first order. Second-order effects at the roof level were checked separately and
were found not to govern for a single-storey building of this height and stiffness.
7.5 Because the diaphragm's in-plane stiffness depends on the deck design, the model was run over the range of
G' available from the deck catalogue for the 6 ft-0 in span. The distribution of force to the frames, the diaphragm
shear field and the deflection reported by the deck designer are to be taken from a model run at the G' of the deck
actually selected, not at an assumed value.
8 What the deck diaphragm design is to report
8.1 For each lateral case - wind along each axis including the torsional case, and seismic along each axis including
accidental torsion - the deck design is to report the maximum in-plane shear in the deck in pounds per linear foot,
the maximum in-plane deflection of the diaphragm in inches, the maximum chord force and the maximum collector
force in kips.
8.2 The chord force to be reported is the largest axial force in the chord line for that direction, taken from the
in-plane model of clause 6.3: the chord lines are the two perimeter lines parallel to the span of the diaphragm, and
the reported value is the largest axial force anywhere along them. The deep-beam value, the in-plane moment at a
section divided by the distance between the chords, is a check on that result and not the quantity reported: in a
semi-rigid diaphragm the perimeter line shares the chord force with the framing on it, so the two differ.
8.2.1 The collector force to be reported is the largest axial force in a perimeter member within one bay of a
braced frame of that direction, again from the in-plane model; it is amplified by Omega_0 before it is compared
with the capacity of Table 6-1.

with hd taken as zero if the expression is negative. A fetch shorter than 20 ft is taken as lu = 20 ft; there is no upper
limit on lu other than the roof itself.
5.4.2 Surcharge shape. A drift forming against an obstruction of clear height hc = h - hb is triangular, with its peak
at the face of the obstruction and falling linearly to zero at the far edge of the drift. Where hd is not greater than hc
the drift is full height: the peak surcharge is hd x gamma and the drift width is w = 4 hd. Where hd exceeds hc the
drift is truncated by the obstruction: the peak surcharge is hc x gamma and the width is w = min(4 hd^2 / hc, 8 hc).
The surcharge is added to the balanced load pf, and the balanced load acts over the whole roof including beneath
the drift.
5.4.3 Windward face. On the face that the wind arrives at, a windward drift of height 0.75 hd is taken, with lu
equal to the roof fetch from the upwind roof edge to that face.
5.4.4 Sheltered face. On the sheltered face, a leeward drift of height hd is taken, with lu equal to the along-wind
length of the obstruction itself, that is, the dimension of the obstruction measured in the direction the wind is
blowing. The roof of the obstruction is the snow source for that drift.
5.4.5 Wind directions. Wind is considered from each of the four directions in turn. Every obstruction forms a
windward drift on the face the wind arrives at and a leeward drift on its sheltered face in each direction. The design
surcharge at a point on the roof is the largest of the surcharges produced at that point by the four directions; the
four directions are not superimposed.
5.4.6 Parapets. A parapet is treated by the windward rule of clause 5.4.3: the drift height is 0.75 hd with lu equal to
the roof dimension upwind of the parapet, and the clear height is hc = parapet height above the roof surface minus
hb. The parapet on this project is 3 ft-6 in high on all four sides.
5.4.7 Application to the deck. The deck is a local element. Each deck zone must carry the peak surcharge
occurring anywhere within the area it serves, not the average over that area and not the value at its centre.
Where a drift crosses a zone boundary the higher demand governs the whole of the zone it falls in.
5.5 Snow buildup at rooftop obstructions
Per UFC 3-301-01 paragraph 3-4.1, which adopts ASCE 7-22 Section 7.4 [Supplement], snow buildup around
rooftop obstructions is to be considered. Rooftop equipment, equipment curbs, equipment enclosures and screen
walls are obstructions. An obstruction standing more than 2.0 ft above the balanced snow surface (that is, hc
greater than 2.0 ft) is treated as a drift obstruction and is given the full treatment of clause 5.4 on every face.
Shorter obstructions need not be given a drift surcharge, but the balanced load is carried across them.
5.5.1 The equipment enclosure, the equipment screen wall and the packaged rooftop units shown on the current
revision of the rooftop equipment plan and in the roof structure model are all obstructions within the meaning of this
clause. Their plan position and height are to be taken from the current revision of those documents.

Permanent floor means a structurally completed floor at any level or elevation (including slab on grade).

Personal fall arrest system means a system used to arrest an employee in a fall from a working level. A personal fall arrest system consists of an anchorage, connectors, a body harness and may include a lanyard, deceleration device, lifeline, or suitable combination of these. The use of a body belt for fall arrest is prohibited.

Positioning device system means a body belt or body harness rigged to allow an employee to be supported on an elevated, vertical surface, such as a wall or column and work with both hands free while leaning.

Post means a structural member with a longitudinal axis that is essentially vertical, that: (1) weighs 300 pounds or less and is axially loaded (a load presses down on the top end), or (2) is not axially loaded, but is laterally restrained by the above member. Posts typically support stair landings, wall framing, mezzanines and other substructures.

Project structural engineer of record means the registered, licensed professional responsible for the design of structural steel framing and whose seal appears on the structural contract documents.

Purlin (in systems-engineered metal buildings) means a “Z” or “C” shaped member formed from sheet steel spanning between primary framing and supporting roof material.

Qualified person (also defined in § 1926.32) means one who, by possession of a recognized degree, certificate, or professional standing, or who by extensive knowledge, training, and experience, has successfully demonstrated the ability to solve or resolve problems relating to the subject matter, the work, or the project.

Safety deck attachment means an initial attachment that is used to secure an initially placed sheet of decking to keep proper alignment and bearing with structural support members.

Shear connector means headed steel studs, steel bars, steel lugs, and similar devices which are attached to a structural member for the purpose of achieving composite action with concrete.

Steel erection means the construction, alteration or repair of steel buildings, bridges and other structures, including the installation of metal decking and all planking used during the process of erection.

Steel joist means an open web, secondary load-carrying member of 144 feet (43.9 m) or less, designed by the manufacturer, used for the support of floors and roofs. This does not include structural steel trusses or cold-formed joists.

Steel joist girder means an open web, primary load-carrying member, designed by the manufacturer, used for the support of floors and roofs. This does not include structural steel trusses.

Steel truss means an open web member designed of structural steel components by the project structural engineer of record. For the purposes of this subpart, a steel truss is considered equivalent to a solid web structural member.

Structural steel means a steel member, or a member made of a substitute material (such as, but not limited to, fiberglass, aluminum or composite members). These members include, but are not limited to, steel joists, joist girders, purlins, columns, beams, trusses, splices, seats, metal decking, girts, and all bridging, and cold formed metal framing which is integrated with the structural steel framing of a building.

Systems-engineered metal building means a metal, field-assembled building system consisting of framing, roof and wall coverings. Typically, many of these components are cold-formed shapes. These individual parts are fabricated in one or more manufacturing facilities and shipped to the job site for assembly into the final structure. The engineering design of the system is normally the responsibility of the systems-engineered metal building manufacturer.

Tank means a container for holding gases, liquids or solids.

Unprotected sides and edges means any side or edge (except at entrances to points of access) of a walking/working surface, for example a, floor, roof, ramp or runway, where there is no wall or guardrail system at least 39 inches (1.0 m) high.

Shear connectors (such as headed steel studs, steel bars or steel lugs), reinforcing bars, deformed anchors or threaded studs shall not be attached to the top flanges of beams, joists or beam attachments so that they project vertically from or horizontally across the top flange of the member until after the metal decking, or other walking/working surface, has been installed.

Hall A is a single-storey warehouse and cross-dock building of 120 ft by 90 ft on plan on the Continental Drive site
in Butte. The roof framing is open-web joists at 5 ft-6 in on centre spanning 40 ft-0 in to hot-rolled girders on the
interior column lines. There is no parapet: the roof is edged with a gutter and a fascia, and there is no rooftop
equipment other than four gravity ridge ventilators. The building is Risk Category II.

2.1 Drift surcharges were taken at the two ridge ventilator banks and at the stepped roof over the office annex. No
other obstruction on this roof is tall enough to form a drift.
3 Deck selection
3.1 The roof deck is Cascade C-30 narrow-rib deck, 1-1/2 in depth, 30 in cover width, 22 gage throughout, laid
in three-span lengths across the joists.
3.2 The support attachment is 36/4 at every support over the whole roof, with button punch at 24 in centres. A
single deck specification was carried across the building; no zoning was used and none was needed, the
diaphragm demand being low and uniform.
3.3 The diaphragm was checked as flexible, spanning between the end wall braced bays. The maximum
diaphragm shear was 205 plf under wind and 96 plf under seismic; the chord was the continuous eave angle.
4 Notes for future reference
4.1 This summary records the design of Hall A on the Continental Drive site in Butte and applies to that building
only. The loads, the deck gage, the attachment pattern and the diaphragm results above are particular to that
building, its site, its exposure and its risk category. They are not transferable to another building, another site or
another risk category, and are not to be used as a starting point for one.

overlay. Minimum roof live loads are taken from UFC 3-301-01 Table E-1.
1.2 Thermal effects are excluded from the roof deck design by agreement with the authority having jurisdiction.
2 Risk category and importance factors
2.1 The facility is Risk Category III. Is = 1.10 for snow and Ie = 1.25 for seismic.
3 Dead loads
3.1 Roofing, insulation and cover board 4.5 psf; suspended mechanical, electrical and plumbing allowance 6.0 psf;
deck self weight per the deck catalogue for the gage used.
4 Roof live load
4.1 Roof live load is taken from UFC 3-301-01 Table E-1. For an ordinary flat roof the unreduced value is Lo = 20
psf.
4.2 The tributary-area and slope reductions Lr = Lo R1 R2 are applied to the roof framing and to the roof deck alike,
subject to the floor value of the reduction. The deck is designed for the reduced roof live load Lr = 12 psf.
4.3 Roof live load is not combined with snow load.
5 Snow loads
5.1 pf = 0.7 Ce Ct Is pg, with pg = 63 psf from the site-specific case study, Ce = 0.90 and Ct = 1.0, giving pf = 43.66
psf.
5.2 Snow density gamma = 0.13 pg + 14, not greater than 30 pcf; gamma = 22.19 pcf.
5.3 Balanced snow depth hb = pf / gamma = 1.968 ft.

def drift_profile(h_obs, hd_raw):

# Roof Deck Structural Design Basis — DC-2 Helena Data Centre, Building A

**Project Number:** DC2-2026-014  
**Facility:** DC-2 Helena Data Centre — Building A (Lewis and Clark County, Montana; Elevation 4,880 ft)  
**Owner:** Continental Divide Digital Infrastructure LLC  
**Structural Engineer of Record:** Sandalwood Marlow Structural Engineers, PLLC  
**Record Date:** 31 July 2026  

---

## 1. Governing Documents and Conflict Resolution

Per Document Transmittal **T-118** and the Owner's Basis of Design (**OBD-DC2-A Rev A**), the following hierarchy and conflict resolutions govern the roof deck design:

1. **Structural Design Criteria (`EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2`, issued 31 July 2026) vs. Archive `Rev 1` (15 May 2026):**
   - `EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2` supersedes `Rev 1` in its entirety. Key changes enforced from `Rev 2` include: (a) inclusion of 20% of the flat-roof snow load ($0.20 p_f$) in the effective seismic weight $w_{seismic}$ because $p_f = 43.66\text{ psf} > 30\text{ psf}$ (Clause 7.2); (b) LRFD diaphragm shear resistance factors $\phi_d = 0.65$ for wind and $\phi_d = 0.60$ for seismic (Clause 9.1, replacing the flat 0.70 in Rev 1); (c) practical zoning caps of $\le 2$ gages, $\le 3$ attachment patterns, $\le 12$ zones, and $\le 14$ rectangles with minimum $18\text{ ft} \times 18\text{ ft}$ dimensions except where truncated by a framed roof opening (Clause 10.2); and (d) minimum `36/7` support pattern and $\ge 3$ sidelap connectors per span for any zone abutting the roof perimeter or a framed roof opening (Clause 10.3).
2. **3D Structural BIM (`DC2-A-STR_Roof_Structure_Model_RevC.ifc`) vs. 2D Drawings (`A-201 Rev C`, `A-201 Rev B`, `M-401 Rev C`, `S-101 Rev 3`, `S-501 Rev 2`):**

## 3. Diaphragm Analysis and Classification

The roof diaphragm was analysed using the 2D finite-element formulation defined in `LAT-2026-003` and `EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2`:
- $40 \times 6 = 240$ pure-shear panels ($6\text{ ft} \times 30\text{ ft}$), where the five $6\text{ ft} \times 6\text{ ft}$ deck strips across each $30\text{ ft}$ girder bay act in series ($G'_{panel} = 5 / \sum (1/G'_k)$), and panels containing framed openings (`RO-1` at $[96,108]\times[48,60]$, `RO-2` at $[132,144]\times[120,132]$, `RO-3` at $[180,210]\times[60,84]$) are modelled as holes in the shear field.
- Axial bar elements along all 41 joist lines ($EA_{joist} = 87,580\text{ kip}$) and all 7 girder lines ($EA_{girder} = 221,850\text{ kip}$), augmented along the four perimeter lines by the continuous `L5x3-1/2x5/16` edge member ($EA_{edge} = 74,240\text{ kip}$).
- Braced frames modelled as elastic springs with half of each frame's roof-level stiffness at each of its two column nodes (`BF-X1, X2`: $55.0\text{ kip/in}$ each on Grid A; `BF-X3, X4`: $18.0\text{ kip/in}$ each on Grid G; `BF-Y1, Y2`: $22.0\text{ kip/in}$ each on Grid 1; `BF-Y3, Y4`: $68.0\text{ kip/in}$ each on Grid 9). Regularisation springs carry $< 0.01\%$ of the applied force (well below the $2\%$ threshold).

### 3.1 Diaphragm Classification (`SEMI-RIGID`)
Under the governing seismic lateral load ($F_{px} = 195.43\text{ kip}$), the average storey drift of the vertical braced frames is $\Delta_{ADVE,X} = 1.56\text{ in}$ (so $2.0 \Delta_{ADVE,X} = 3.12\text{ in}$) and $\Delta_{ADVE,Y} = 1.42\text{ in}$ (so $2.0 \Delta_{ADVE,Y} = 2.84\text{ in}$). The maximum computed in-plane diaphragm deflection is $0.715\text{ in}$ in X (`S07`/`S10`) and $1.079\text{ in}$ in Y (`S08`), both well below $2.0 \Delta_{ADVE}$ and below the $1.60\text{ in}$ serviceability cap of Clause 9.2. Accordingly, the diaphragm is classified as **`SEMI-RIGID`**.

## 4. Zoning Decisions and Installed Cost Summary

To satisfy all gravity snow-drift, wind uplift, diaphragm shear, deflection, chord/collector splice, and constructability rules at minimum installed cost, the roof is divided into **4 zones** across **14 rectangles** (covering all $42,192\text{ sq ft}$ of decked roof area, excluding the $1,008\text{ sq ft}$ of cells touched by `RO-1`, `RO-2`, and `RO-3`), using **2 deck gages** (22 gage and 18 gage) and **3 attachment patterns**:

## 3. Diaphragm Analysis and Classification

The roof diaphragm was analysed using the 2D finite-element formulation defined in `LAT-2026-003` and `EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2`:
- $40 \times 6 = 240$ pure-shear panels ($6\text{ ft} \times 30\text{ ft}$), where the five $6\text{ ft} \times 6\text{ ft}$ deck strips across each $30\text{ ft}$ girder bay act in series ($G'_{panel} = 5 / \sum (1/G'_k)$), and panels containing framed openings (`RO-1` at $[96,108]\times[48,60]$, `RO-2` at $[132,144]\times[120,132]$, `RO-3` at $[180,210]\times[60,84]$) are modelled as holes in the shear field.
- Axial bar elements along all 41 joist lines ($EA_{joist} = 87,580\text{ kip}$) and all 7 girder lines ($EA_{girder} = 221,850\text{ kip}$), augmented along the four perimeter lines by the continuous `L5x3-1/2x5/16` edge member ($EA_{edge} = 74,240\text{ kip}$).

  1: # Roof Deck Structural Design Basis — DC-2 Helena Data Centre, Building A
  2: 
  3: **Project Number:** DC2-2026-014  
  4: **Facility:** DC-2 Helena Data Centre — Building A (Lewis and Clark County, Montana; Elevation 4,880 ft)  
  5: **Owner:** Continental Divide Digital Infrastructure LLC  
  6: **Structural Engineer of Record:** Sandalwood Marlow Structural Engineers, PLLC  
  7: **Record Date:** 31 July 2026  
  8: 
  9: ---
 10: 
 11: ## 1. Governing Documents and Conflict Resolution
 12: 
 13: Per Document Transmittal **T-118** and the Owner's Basis of Design (**OBD-DC2-A Rev A**), the following hierarchy and conflict resolutions govern the roof deck design:
 14: 
 15: 1. **Structural Design Criteria (`EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2`, issued 31 July 2026) vs. Archive `Rev 1` (15 May 2026):**
 16:    - `EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2` supersedes `Rev 1` in its entirety. Key changes enforced from `Rev 2` include: (a) inclusion of 20% of the flat-roof snow load ($0.20 p_f$) in the effective seismic weight $w_{seismic}$ because $p_f = 43.66\text{ psf} > 30\text{ psf}$ (Clause 7.2); (b) LRFD diaphragm shear resistance factors $\phi_d = 0.65$ for wind and $\phi_d = 0.60$ for seismic (Clause 9.1, replacing the flat 0.70 in Rev 1); (c) practical zoning caps of $\le 2$ gages, $\le 3$ attachment patterns, $\le 12$ zones, and $\le 14$ rectangles with minimum $18\text{ ft} \times 18\text{ ft}$ dimensions except where truncated by a framed roof opening (Clause 10.2); and (d) minimum `36/7` support pattern and $\ge 3$ sidelap connectors per span for any zone abutting the roof perimeter or a framed roof opening (Clause 10.3).
 17: 2. **3D Structural BIM (`DC2-A-STR_Roof_Structure_Model_RevC.ifc`) vs. 2D Drawings (`A-201 Rev C`, `A-201 Rev B`, `M-401 Rev C`, `S-101 Rev 3`, `S-501 Rev 2`):**
 18:    - Per **T-118** Note 2 and **EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2** Clause 1.3, the 3D structural model (`Rev C`) is the authoritative geometric record of the building framing, framed openings, and rooftop obstructions.
 19:    - Superseded architectural plan `A-201 Rev B` showed the north equipment screen `SCR-N` at $y = 158\text{ ft}$ ($16\text{ ft}$ from the north parapet) and is excluded. Both `DC2-A-STR Rev C.ifc` and `A-201 Rev C` place `SCR-N` at $y = 164.0\text{ ft}$ ($x \in [18, 222]\text{ ft}$, $h = 6.0\text{ ft}$) and `SCR-E` at $x = 216.0\text{ ft}$ ($y \in [24, 144]\text{ ft}$, $h = 7.0\text{ ft}$).
 20:    - While `A-201 Rev C` labels the rooftop equipment enclosure `MEP-PH-1` ($x \in [60, 180]\text{ ft}$, $y \in [60, 120]\text{ ft}$, $h = 12.0\text{ ft}$) as "open top", **EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2** Clauses 5.4.4, 5.4.5, and 5.5.1 explicitly mandate that the roof of every obstruction be treated as the snow source for leeward drifts with $l_u$ equal to the along-wind dimension of the obstruction ($120\text{ ft}$ EW, $60\text{ ft}$ NS) and applied exactly as written.
 21: 3. **Site-Specific Ground Snow Study (`SNOW-2026-014`) vs. Mapped Values:**
 22:    - Per **OBD-DC2-A** Section 3.2 and **EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2** Clause 5.1, the site-specific case study (`SNOW-2026-014`, $p_g = 63.0\text{ psf}$) governs exclusively over regional mapped values.
 23: 4. **Seismic Hazard (`USGS_ASCE7-22_RC-III_SiteClass-D` vs. 2019 Preliminary Report):**
 24:    - The 2026 ASCE 7-22 Risk Category III, Site Class D report ($S_{DS} = 0.44$, $S_{D1} = 0.24$, $I_e = 1.25$) governs; the 2019 preliminary ASCE 7-16 Risk Category II Site Class C report is superseded and excluded.
 25: 5. **Deck Product and Procurement (`NORDECK B-36 2026 Catalogue`, `Deck_Stock_Availability_2026-07`, `Cost_Plan_CP-RD-2026` vs. 2019 Hall A Butte Reference):**
 26:    - The 2019 Hall A Butte reference design is an archive warehouse design using a discontinued product and does not apply.
 27:    - Per **OBD-DC2-A** Section 5.1 and **EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2** Clause 11.2, deck material must be available on site within **9 weeks** of release. Per `Deck_Stock_Availability_2026-07.xlsx`, 22 gage (2 weeks), 20 gage (3 weeks), and 18 gage (4 weeks) meet the 9-week limit, whereas **16 gage** (14 weeks mill rolling) violates the 9-week cap and is prohibited.
 28: 
 29: ---
 30: 
 31: ## 1.A Scope Exclusions and Fixed Boundary Conditions
 32: 
 33: - Thermal effects are excluded from the roof deck design (roof assembly is fully insulated above the deck and building is conditioned continuously; AHJ agreed self-straining thermal forces need not be combined with gravity, snow, wind or seismic effects).
 34: - Roof framing (open-web steel joists at 6 ft-0 in o.c. spanning 30 ft between joist girders over 240 ft x 180 ft footprint) is fixed and not to be changed.
 35: - Ponding instability is addressed by drainage design (internal drains with secondary overflow scuppers) and by deck stiffness requirements of the structural design criteria.
 36: 
 37: ---
 38: 
 39: ## 2. Gravity, Snow Drift, Uplift, and Seismic Load Basis
 40: 
 41: ### 2.1 Dead Load ($D$) and Roof Live Load ($L_r$ — Scenario `S01`)
 42: - **Superimposed Dead Load:** $4.5\text{ psf}$ (roofing/insulation) $+ 6.0\text{ psf}$ (suspended MEP allowance) $= 10.5\text{ psf}$.
 43: - **Deck Self-Weight:** $1.6\text{ psf}$ for 22 gage ($D = 12.1\text{ psf}$); $2.5\text{ psf}$ for 18 gage ($D = 13.0\text{ psf}$).
 44: - **Roof Live Load ($L_r$):** $20.0\text{ psf}$ unreduced on the roof deck (**UFC 3-301-01** Table E-1 Item 51, **EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2** Clause 4.2).
 45: 
 46: ### 2.2 Balanced Snow and Snow Drifts (Scenarios `S02`, `S03`, `S04`)
 47: - **Ground Snow Load:** $p_g = 63.0\text{ psf}$ (`SNOW-2026-014`).
 48: - **Flat-Roof Snow Load:**With $C_e = 0.90$, $C_t = 1.00$, $I_s = 1.10$ (Risk Category III):
 49:   $$p_f = 0.7 C_e C_t I_s p_g = 0.7(0.90)(1.00)(1.10)(63.0) = 43.66\text{ psf}$$
 50: - **Snow Density and Balanced Depth:**
 51:   $$\gamma = \min(0.13 p_g + 14, 30) = 22.19\text{ pcf}, \quad h_b = \frac{p_f}{\gamma} = 1.968\text{ ft}$$
 52: - **Drift Methodology (Clause 5.4):** For upwind fetch $l_u \ge 20\text{ ft}$, $h_d = 0.43 l_u^{1/3}(p_g + 10)^{1/4} - 1.5\text{ ft}$ (leeward) and $0.75 h_d$ (windward and parapets). Where $h_d \le h_c = h - h_b$, peak surcharge $p_d = h_d \gamma$ and width $w = 4 h_d$; where $h_d > h_c$, $p_d = h_c \gamma$ and $w = \min(4 h_d^2 / h_c, 8 h_c)$.
 53: - **Key Scheduled Drifts (`Drifts` Sheet):**
 54:   - **`MEP-PH-1` Face `W` ($x = 60.0\text{ ft}$, $h = 12.0\text{ ft}$, $h_c = 10.032\text{ ft}$):** Governed by East-wind leeward drift ($l_u = 120\text{ ft}$, $h_d = 4.700\text{ ft} < h_c$), giving $p_d = 104.28\text{ psf}$ and width $w = 18.80\text{ ft}$ ($x \in [41.20, 60.0]\text{ ft}$).
 55:   - **`SCR-N` Face `S` ($y = 164.0\text{ ft}$, $h = 6.0\text{ ft}$, $h_c = 4.032\text{ ft}$):** Governed by South-wind windward drift ($l_u = 164.0\text{ ft}$, $0.75 h_d = 4.035\text{ ft} > h_c$), truncated at $h_c = 4.0324\text{ ft}$, giving $p_d = 89.48\text{ psf}$ and width $w = 16.15\text{ ft}$ ($y \in [147.85, 164.0]\text{ ft}$).
 56:   - **`PARAPET` Face `N` ($y = 180.0\text{ ft}$, $h = 3.5\text{ ft}$, $h_c = 1.532\text{ ft}$):** Governed by South-wind windward drift ($l_u = 180.0\text{ ft}$, $0.75 h_d = 4.198\text{ ft} > h_c$), truncated at $h_c = 1.5324\text{ ft}$ with width $w = 8 h_c = 12.26\text{ ft}$, giving $p_d = 34.01\text{ psf}$ ($y \in [167.74, 180.0]\text{ ft}$).
 57:   - **`RTU-1` Face `E` ($x = 36.0\text{ ft}$, $h = 7.0\text{ ft}$, $h_c = 5.032\text{ ft}$):** Governed by East-wind windward drift ($l_u = 204.0\text{ ft}$, $0.75 h_d = 4.424\text{ ft} < h_c$), giving $p_d = 98.17\text{ psf}$ and width $w = 17.70\text{ ft}$ ($x \in [36.0, 53.70]\text{ ft}$).
 58: 
 59: ### 2.3 Components and Cladding Wind Uplift (Scenario `S09`)
 60: - Velocity pressure at $h = 32\text{ ft}$: $q_h = 0.00256 (1.04)(1.0)(0.85)(115)^2 = 29.93\text{ psf}$.
 61: - Edge band width $a = \min(0.1 \times 180, 0.4 \times 32) = 12.8\text{ ft}$, $2a = 25.6\text{ ft}$.
 62: - Gross wind uplift demand $|q_h(GC_p - GC_{pi})|$ is $101.2\text{ psf}$ in Zone 3 (corners), $74.2\text{ psf}$ in Zone 2 (perimeter), $47.3\text{ psf}$ in Zone 1 ($a$ to $2a$), and $32.3\text{ psf}$ in Zone 1' (interior).
 63: - Resisted by $0.9(4.5 + w_{self})$ plus support fastener pull-over capacity $\phi_t P_{nov} / (18/n)$ with $\phi_t = 0.50$. Corner Zone 3 ($101.2\text{ psf}$) requires 18 gage with `36/9` ($119.75 + 6.30 = 126.05\text{ psf}$ capacity).
 64: 
 65: ### 2.4 Wind and Seismic Lateral Loads (Scenarios `S05`, `S06`, `S07`, `S08`, `S10`)
 66: - **Roof-Level Wind Forces (`LAT-2026-003` Table 4-1):** $V_{wind,x} = 118.0\text{ kip}$ (`S05`), $V_{wind,y} = 152.0\text{ kip}$ (`S06`), checked for both Case 1 (100% force, balanced) and Case 2 (75% force with $\pm 0.15 L_{perp}$ torsional eccentricity).
 67: - **Effective Seismic Weight and Force (`LAT-2026-003` Section 5 & `EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2` Clause 7):**
 68:   $$w_{seismic} = 18.0 + 0.20(43.66) = 26.732\text{ psf}$$
 69:   $$W = 26.732 \times 240 \times 180 / 1000 = 1,154.82\text{ kip}, \quad C_s = \frac{S_{DS} I_e}{R} = \frac{0.44 \times 1.25}{3.25} = 0.16923$$
 70:   $$F_{px} = C_s W = 195.43\text{ kip}$$
 71:   Applied with accidental torsional eccentricity $e = \pm 0.05 L_{perp}$ ($\pm 9.0\text{ ft}$ for X in `S07`/`S10`, $\pm 12.0\text{ ft}$ for Y in `S08`), and collector forces amplified by $\Omega_0 = 2.0$ in `S10`.
 72: 
 73: ---
 74: 
 75: ## 3. Diaphragm Analysis and Classification
 76: 
 77: The roof diaphragm was analysed using the 2D finite-element formulation defined in `LAT-2026-003` and `EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2`:
 78: - $40 \times 6 = 240$ pure-shear panels ($6\text{ ft} \times 30\text{ ft}$), where the five $6\text{ ft} \times 6\text{ ft}$ deck strips across each $30\text{ ft}$ girder bay act in series ($G'_{panel} = 5 / \sum (1/G'_k)$), and panels containing framed openings (`RO-1` at $[96,108]\times[48,60]$, `RO-2` at $[132,144]\times[120,132]$, `RO-3` at $[180,210]\times[60,84]$) are modelled as holes in the shear field.
 79: - Axial bar elements along all 41 joist lines ($EA_{joist} = 87,580\text{ kip}$) and all 7 girder lines ($EA_{girder} = 221,850\text{ kip}$), augmented along the four perimeter lines by the continuous `L5x3-1/2x5/16` edge member ($EA_{edge} = 74,240\text{ kip}$).
 80: - Braced frames modelled as elastic springs with half of each frame's roof-level stiffness at each of its two column nodes (`BF-X1, X2`: $55.0\text{ kip/in}$ each on Grid A; `BF-X3, X4`: $18.0\text{ kip/in}$ each on Grid G; `BF-Y1, Y2`: $22.0\text{ kip/in}$ each on Grid 1; `BF-Y3, Y4`: $68.0\text{ kip/in}$ each on Grid 9). Regularisation springs carry $< 0.01\%$ of the applied force (well below the $2\%$ threshold).
 81: 
 82: ### 3.1 Diaphragm Classification (`SEMI-RIGID`)
 83: Under the governing seismic lateral load ($F_{px} = 195.43\text{ kip}$), the average storey drift of the vertical braced frames is $\Delta_{ADVE,X} = 1.56\text{ in}$ (so $2.0 \Delta_{ADVE,X} = 3.12\text{ in}$) and $\Delta_{ADVE,Y} = 1.42\text{ in}$ (so $2.0 \Delta_{ADVE,Y} = 2.84\text{ in}$). The maximum computed in-plane diaphragm deflection is $0.715\text{ in}$ in X (`S07`/`S10`) and $1.079\text{ in}$ in Y (`S08`), both well below $2.0 \Delta_{ADVE}$ and below the $1.60\text{ in}$ serviceability cap of Clause 9.2. Accordingly, the diaphragm is classified as **`SEMI-RIGID`**.
 84: 
 85: ### 3.2 Diaphragm Results Summary
 86: | Scenario | Direction | Max Shear (plf) | Max Deflection (in) | Chord Force (kip) | Collector Force (kip) | Classification |
 87: |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
 88: | `S05` | X | 334.7 | 0.394 | 9.62 | 14.42 | `SEMI-RIGID` |
 89: | `S06` | Y | 726.5 | 0.845 | 27.97 | 16.37 | `SEMI-RIGID` |
 90: | `S07` | X | 550.1 | 0.626 | 16.33 | 28.63 | `SEMI-RIGID` |
 91: | `S08` | Y | 992.5 | 1.079 | 36.32 | 20.89 | `SEMI-RIGID` |
 92: | `S10` | X | 550.1 | 0.626 | 16.33 | 57.25 | `SEMI-RIGID` |
 93: 
 94: Both the maximum chord force ($36.32\text{ kip} \le 38.0\text{ kip}$ splice capacity) and the overstrength-amplified collector force in `S10` ($57.25\text{ kip} \le 58.0\text{ kip}$ splice capacity) satisfy Clause 6.2.1 of `LAT-2026-003`.
 95: 
 96: ---
 97: 
 98: ## 4. Zoning Decisions and Installed Cost Summary
 99: 
100: To satisfy all gravity snow-drift, wind uplift, diaphragm shear, deflection, chord/collector splice, and constructability rules at minimum installed cost, the roof is divided into **4 zones** across **14 rectangles** (covering all $42,192\text{ sq ft}$ of decked roof area, excluding the $1,008\text{ sq ft}$ of cells touched by `RO-1`, `RO-2`, and `RO-3`), using **2 deck gages** (22 gage and 18 gage) and **3 attachment patterns**:
101: 
102: 1. **Zone `Z1` (22 gage, `36/9`, `SCREW-10`, 4 per span — 3 rectangles, $8,712\text{ sq ft}$):**
103:    - Covers the South ($[18,210]\times[0,24]$) and West ($[0,24]\times[24,48]$ and $[0,42]\times[48,132]$) low-drift perimeter regions where balanced snow plus parapet/equipment drift is $\le 91.4\text{ psf}$ (gravity D/C $= 0.976$ in `S04`). The `36/9` support pattern provides $79.99\text{ psf}$ uplift resistance for Perimeter Zone 2 ($74.2\text{ psf}$, D/C $= 0.928$) and $\phi_d S_n = 595.2\text{ plf}$ seismic shear capacity vs. $567.2\text{ plf}$ demand (D/C $= 0.953$).
104: 2. **Zone `Z2` (22 gage, `36/7`, `SCREW-10`, 4 per span — 1 rectangle, $6,840\text{ sq ft}$):**
105:    - Covers the interior of the equipment enclosure (`[66,180]x[60,120]`), where snow drifts form outward from the enclosure walls leaving balanced snow inside, and uplift is Zone 1' ($32.3\text{ psf}$). Uses `36/7` with 4 `SCREW-10` connectors per span ($G' = 22.0\text{ kip/in}$, $\phi_d S_n = 518.4\text{ plf}$), satisfying Clause 10.3 at opening boundaries.
106: 3. **Zone `Z3` (18 gage, `36/7`, `SCREW-10`, 4 per span — 7 rectangles, $12,384\text{ sq ft}$):**
107:    - Covers all interior snow-drift bands around `MEP-PH-1`, `RTU-1` through `RTU-12`, and the framed openings `RO-1`, `RO-2`, and `RO-3`, where peak snow load reaches $147.94\text{ psf}$ ($D + S = 160.94\text{ psf} \le 177.0\text{ psf}$, gravity D/C $= 0.909$ in `S02`). Shares the same attachment pattern (`36/7`, `SCREW-10`, 4) as `Z2` to eliminate an extra pattern set-up charge while providing $G' = 33.8\text{ kip/in}$ and $\phi_d S_n = 775.8\text{ plf}$ vs. $624.8\text{ plf}$ shear demand.

=== OBD-DC2-A ===
Owner's Basis of Design - Excerpt
Document OBD-DC2-A, Revision A. Extract of Sections 1, 3, 5 and 9 issued to the design and construction team for the roof structure package.
1  Project identification
3  Facility description
The building is a single-storey, single-occupancy data centre of 240 ft by 180 ft on plan, framed in structural steel, with the top of roof steel at elevation 32 ft-0 in above finished floor and a continuous 3 ft-6 in parapet on all four sides. The facility supports a designated emergency operations tenant and is therefore classified Risk Category III; the Owner requires that the classification be carried through every load case, including the roof snow and lateral cases, and that it not be traded away in value engineering.
A louvred equipment enclosure and a row of packaged rooftop units stand on the main roof within a screened yard. The roof structure runs continuously beneath the enclosure; the enclosure is not a separate roof level.
3.4  Roof framing and roof deck
The roof framing is open-web steel joists at 6 ft-0 in on centre spanning 30 ft-0 in between joist girders on the transverse column lines. The joist girders are supported on the perimeter columns and on the interior column lines.
The roof deck is to be 1.5 in wide-rib (Type B) steel deck of 3 ft-0 in cover width, spanning across the joists in continuous lengths of not less than three spans wherever the framing allows. The deck serves three functions at once - it carries the roof gravity load to the joists, it acts as the roof diaphragm delivering wind and seismic force to the braced frames, and it is the substrate for the roofing assembly - and the Owner expects a single deck package to satisfy all three.
Deck gage, support attachment and sidelap connection are to be developed by the structural engineer of record and are to be shown on the roof deck drawing as zones, so that the erector can set out the work without reference to a calculation package.
5  Programme and procurement
The roof structure package is on the critical path. The Owner's procurement strategy assumes that roof-deck material is on site and available to the erector within 9 weeks of release for fabrication. A deck product, gage or finish that cannot meet that allowance is not available to this project, whatever its structural merit, and the design is to be developed accordingly.
Release for fabrication of the roof deck package: on approval of the roof deck drawing and the deck attachment schedule.
Material on site: not later than 9 weeks after that release.
Substitutions that lengthen the delivery are to be raised with the Owner before they are carried into the design, not after.
9  Design exclusions and agreements with the authority having jurisdiction
The following have been agreed with the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) in the pre-application review and are recorded here so that they are not re-opened:
Thermal effects are excluded from the roof deck design. The roof assembly is fully insulated above the deck and the building is conditioned continuously; the AHJ has agreed that self-straining thermal forces need not be combined with the gravity, snow, wind or seismic effects in the design of the roof deck and its attachments.
The ground snow load for the site is established by a site-specific case study rather than by the mapped value. The study is a separate document and is the only source of the ground snow load for this project.
Roof drainage is by internal drains with secondary overflow scuppers through the parapet; ponding instability is addressed by the drainage design and by the deck stiffness requirements of the structural design criteria.
Nothing in this excerpt relieves the structural engineer of record of the obligation to apply the importance factors and load combinations required for Risk Category III.
Related documents
The structural design criteria for the roof, the site-specific ground snow load case study, the lateral analysis report, the architectural roof plan and the roof structure model develop this basis of design. The current revision of each is listed on the project document transmittal; where a document in the project file carries an earlier revision, the revision listed on the current transmittal governs.

1 Purpose and scope
This report establishes the ground snow load, pg, for the site of the DC-2 Helena Data Centre - Building A in Lewis
and Clark County, Montana. The site lies in an area for which the mapped ground snow load is not given and for
which a site-specific case study is required. The study determines the ground snow load only. It does not determine
roof snow loads, does not select exposure or thermal factors, and does not apply an importance factor; those are
the work of the structural engineer of record and are set out in the structural design criteria for the project.
2 Regulatory basis
The study has been carried out in accordance with the requirements for snow load case studies in the building
code adopted by the authority having jurisdiction, as modified for Department of Defense work by UFC 3-301-01,
Structural Engineering. UFC 3-301-01 paragraph 2-4.5 directs the designer to section 1608.2.3, Snow Load Case
Studies, which requires that, where a case study is made, "the ground snow load is to be determined based on a
Risk Category II structure for this purpose".
2.1 Accordingly, the ground snow load reported in section 6 is determined on a Risk Category II basis. It is a site
characteristic, not a structure-specific design value. The structure served by this study is classified in a higher risk
category; the importance factor appropriate to that classification is applied separately by the structural engineer of
record, in the structural design criteria, and has deliberately not been built into the value reported here. Applying an
importance factor to the value reported in section 6 a second time would be an error.
2.2 Exposure, thermal and slope effects, drift surcharges, rain-on-snow surcharge and the minimum roof snow load
are outside the scope of this study.
3 Site description
The site is a broad bench on the west side of the Missouri River valley at an elevation of 4,880 ft, approximately 4
miles west of Canyon Ferry Reservoir. The bench is open and unobstructed, falling gently to the east. The
surrounding terrain rises steeply to the west into the Continental Divide, where the high-elevation snow course and
SNOTEL network provides a long record of seasonal accumulation. Winter precipitation at the site is orographically
enhanced relative to the valley floor stations to the east and north, and the seasonal snowpack is subject to
repeated mid-winter melt and rain-on-snow episodes that consolidate the pack without removing it.

spanning an elevation band from 3,830 ft to 7,000 ft. Records were drawn from the National Weather Service
co-operative network, the Natural Resources Conservation Service SNOTEL network and the state climate office
archive. Station records were checked for homogeneity, gaps were flagged rather than filled, and station values

4.1 The annual maximum water equivalent series for the Canyon Ferry Dam station, the closest station to the site,

below the site and its series is not by itself a determination of the ground snow load for the site.
5 Methodology
The study follows the Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory (CRREL) methodology for
site-specific ground snow loads, as used to develop the mapped values in the national standard and as applied in
the published CRREL state and regional snow load studies. The steps are:
5.1 Assemble the annual maximum ground snow water equivalent at each station over its period of record,
converting measured depth to water equivalent where water equivalent was not observed, using the station's own
measured seasonal density where available.
5.2 Fit a log-normal distribution to each station's annual maxima by the method of moments, and extract the
50-year mean recurrence interval value. The log-normal fit is adopted in preference to the Gumbel fit on the
evidence of the probability plots for the valley stations, which show the characteristic upward curvature of a mixed
rain-on-snow population.
5.3 Convert the 50-year water equivalent to a ground snow load in pounds per square foot at 5.20 psf per inch of
water equivalent.
5.4 Regress the station 50-year loads on station elevation over the local elevation band, weighting each station by
its record length, and evaluate the regression at the site elevation. The regression over the seven stations of Table
4-1 gives a coefficient of determination of 0.96 with a standard error of estimate of 6.4 psf.
5.5 Check the regression value against the two nearest long-record stations after adjusting them to the site
elevation individually, and against the state study value for the same elevation band. Adopt the regression value
where the checks agree within the standard error, as they do here.
5.6 The analysis period is the 45 water years 1981 to 2025 for the regression stations with concurrent record,
extended to the full period of record at each station for the distribution fitting of paragraph 5.2. No trend adjustment

reported in Table 6-1 for use on this project, by letter dated 28 April 2026, subject to the condition that the
importance factor for the structure be applied by the structural engineer of record and that the approval not be
transferred to another site.
8 Limitations
This study applies to the site described in section 3 and to no other. It reports a ground snow load only. It is not a
determination of roof snow load, of drift surcharge or of the minimum roof snow load, and it does not consider the
geometry of any structure. Use of the value reported here on another site, at another elevation, or with an
importance factor already embedded, is outside the scope of this report.

=== OBD-DC2-A ===
Owner's Basis of Design - Excerpt
Document OBD-DC2-A, Revision A. Extract of Sections 1, 3, 5 and 9 issued to the design and construction team for the roof structure package.
1  Project identification
3  Facility description
The building is a single-storey, single-occupancy data centre of 240 ft by 180 ft on plan, framed in structural steel, with the top of roof steel at elevation 32 ft-0 in above finished floor and a continuous 3 ft-6 in parapet on all four sides. The facility supports a designated emergency operations tenant and is therefore classified Risk Category III; the Owner requires that the classification be carried through every load case, including the roof snow and lateral cases, and that it not be traded away in value engineering.
A louvred equipment enclosure and a row of packaged rooftop units stand on the main roof within a screened yard. The roof structure runs continuously beneath the enclosure; the enclosure is not a separate roof level.
3.4  Roof framing and roof deck
The roof framing is open-web steel joists at 6 ft-0 in on centre spanning 30 ft-0 in between joist girders on the transverse column lines. The joist girders are supported on the perimeter columns and on the interior column lines.
The roof deck is to be 1.5 in wide-rib (Type B) steel deck of 3 ft-0 in cover width, spanning across the joists in continuous lengths of not less than three spans wherever the framing allows. The deck serves three functions at once - it carries the roof gravity load to the joists, it acts as the roof diaphragm delivering wind and seismic force to the braced frames, and it is the substrate for the roofing assembly - and the Owner expects a single deck package to satisfy all three.
Deck gage, support attachment and sidelap connection are to be developed by the structural engineer of record and are to be shown on the roof deck drawing as zones, so that the erector can set out the work without reference to a calculation package.
5  Programme and procurement
The roof structure package is on the critical path. The Owner's procurement strategy assumes that roof-deck material is on site and available to the erector within 9 weeks of release for fabrication. A deck product, gage or finish that cannot meet that allowance is not available to this project, whatever its structural merit, and the design is to be developed accordingly.
Release for fabrication of the roof deck package: on approval of the roof deck drawing and the deck attachment schedule.
Material on site: not later than 9 weeks after that release.
Substitutions that lengthen the delivery are to be raised with the Owner before they are carried into the design, not after.
9  Design exclusions and agreements with the authority having jurisdiction
The following have been agreed with the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) in the pre-application review and are recorded here so that they are not re-opened:
Thermal effects are excluded from the roof deck design. The roof assembly is fully insulated above the deck and the building is conditioned continuously; the AHJ has agreed that self-straining thermal forces need not be combined with the gravity, snow, wind or seismic effects in the design of the roof deck and its attachments.
The ground snow load for the site is established by a site-specific case study rather than by the mapped value. The study is a separate document and is the only source of the ground snow load for this project.
Roof drainage is by internal drains with secondary overflow scuppers through the parapet; ponding instability is addressed by the drainage design and by the deck stiffness requirements of the structural design criteria.
Nothing in this excerpt relieves the structural engineer of record of the obligation to apply the importance factors and load combinations required for Risk Category III.
Related documents
The structural design criteria for the roof, the site-specific ground snow load case study, the lateral analysis report, the architectural roof plan and the roof structure model develop this basis of design. The current revision of each is listed on the project document transmittal; where a document in the project file carries an earlier revision, the revision listed on the current transmittal governs.

[P1] DC2-2026-014  DC-2 Helena Data Centre - Building A EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2  -  31 July 2026 Sandalwood Marlow Structural Engineers, PLLC  -  structural design criteria, roof Page 1 Structural Design Criteria - Roof Document EOR-DC-RD-01, Revision 2 Project DC2-2026-014 - DC-2 Helena Data Centre - Building A Site Lewis and Clark County, Montana (Canyon Ferry Road site, elevation 4,880 ft) Structural engineer of record Sandalwood Marlow Structural Engineers, PLLC Scope of this document Loads, load combinations, serviceability limits and deck design rules for the main roof structure and the steel roof deck. Issued 31 July 2026 Rev Date Description Status 2 31 July 2026 Reissued in full. Clause 4.2 (roof live load on the deck) rewritten; clause 5.4 (drift surcharges) rewritten to give the windward and leeward rules and the four wind directions; clause 7.2 (effective seismic weight) rewritten to include the snow contribution; clauses 9.3 and 10.4 added. Current - for construction 1 15 May 2026 First issue for design development. Superseded by Rev 2 Revision record. 1 Codes and standards 1.1 The building code adopted by the authority having jurisdiction is the International Building Code as adopted and amended by the State of Montana and by Lewis and Clark County, together with the referenced standard for minimum design loads and associated criteria for buildings and other structures. All section numbers quoted in this document without another source are sections of that adopted code. 1.2 The Department of Defense criteria overlay for this project is UFC 3-301-01, Structural Engineering. Where UFC 3-301-01 replaces, supplements or adds to a provision of the adopted building code, the UFC provision governs. Clauses of this document that rest on a UFC modification cite the UFC paragraph. 1.3 Minimum roof live loads are taken from UFC 3-301-01 Table E-1, not from the live load table of the adopted code. Where Table E-1 and the adopted code differ, Table E-1 governs. 1.4 Cold-formed steel deck is designed to the North American specification for cold-formed steel structural members; steel deck diaphragms are designed to the North American standard for the design of profiled steel diaphragm panels. Open-web steel joists and joist girders are designed and supplied to the Steel Joist Institute specifications. Hot-rolled steel members are designed to the AISC specification for structural steel buildings. 1.5 Thermal effects are excluded from the design of the roof deck and its attachments by agreement with the authority having jurisdiction, recorded in the Owner's basis of design. Self-straining forces are not combined with the load effects of section 8 of this document. 2 Risk category and importance factors 2.1 The facility is classified Risk Category III. The classification applies to every load case, including the roof snow, wind and seismic cases, and to the roof deck as a component of the structure. Quantity Symbol Value Application Snow importance factor Is 1.10 Applied to the flat roof snow load, clause 5.1 Seismic importance factor Ie 1.25 Applied to the seismic base shear and diaphragm force, clause 7.1 Wind - included in V Risk Category III basic wind speed, clause 6.1 2.2 The ground snow load used in clause 5.1 is taken from the site-specific case study SNOW-2026-014, which reports it on a Risk Category II basis as the case study provisions require. The importance factor Is of Table 2-1 above is the only importance factor applied to it; it is not applied twice.

[P2] DC2-2026-014  DC-2 Helena Data Centre - Building A EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2  -  31 July 2026 Sandalwood Marlow Structural Engineers, PLLC  -  structural design criteria, roof Page 2 3 Dead loads Item Load (psf) Notes Roofing, insulation and cover board 4.5 Single-ply membrane, 3 in polyisocyanurate, cover board Suspended mechanical, electrical and plumbing allowance 6.0 Uniform allowance for services hung from the roof structure Collateral dead load, total 10.5 Excluding deck self weight Steel deck self weight per catalogue Taken from the deck catalogue for the gage used; it varies with gage and is added to the collateral dead load in every gravity and uplift check 3.1 Rooftop equipment is supported on curbs carried by reinforced framing and is not treated as a uniform dead load on the deck. Operating weights are given on the rooftop equipment schedule. 3.2 The roof dead weight used for the seismic effective weight is given in clause 7.2 and is broken down in the lateral analysis report. 4 Roof live load 4.1 Roof live load Lr is taken from UFC 3-301-01 Table E-1. For an ordinary flat roof that is not occupiable and is not a roof garden or an assembly area, Table E-1 item 51 gives an unreduced roof live load of Lo = 20 psf. 4.2 Roof live load on the deck. The tributary-area reduction Lr = Lo R1 R2 applies only where the tributary area exceeds 200 sq ft: for a tributary area At not exceeding 200 sq ft, R1 = 1.0. A deck panel's tributary area is the panel cover width times the joist spacing, 3 ft x 6 ft = 18 sq ft, which is far below the 200 sq ft threshold, so no reduction is available to the deck. The roof deck and its attachments are therefore designed for the unreduced roof live load Lr = 20 psf. The slope reduction R2 is 1.0 for the roof slope used on this project. 4.3 The joists, joist girders and columns take the tributary-area reduction on their own tributary areas, subject to the floor value of Lr = 12 psf. The reduced value is a member-by-member result and is not to be carried back into the deck design; a deck designed for the reduced roof live load is not compliant with this document. 4.4 Roof live load is not combined with snow load; the larger of the two governs in the combinations of section 8. Construction loading is covered by clause 9.1. 5 Snow loads 5.1 Flat roof snow load. pf = 0.7 Ce Ct Is pg, with the ground snow load pg = 63 psf from the site-specific case study SNOW-2026-014, the exposure factor Ce = 0.90 (Terrain Category C, partially exposed roof - the roof carries a continuous parapet, an equipment enclosure and rooftop units), and the thermal factor Ct = 1.0 (heated structure, continuously conditioned). With Is = 1.10 from clause 2.1: pf = 0.7 x 0.90 x 1.00 x 1.10 x 63 = 43.66 psf Because pg exceeds 20 psf, the minimum roof snow load provision does not control and the rain-on-snow surcharge is not required. 5.2 Snow density. gamma = 0.13 pg + 14, not greater than 30 pcf. For this site gamma = 0.13 x 63 + 14 = 22.19 pcf. 5.3 Balanced snow depth. hb = pf / gamma = 43.66 / 22.19 = 1.968 ft. All clear heights used for drift surcharges are measured from the top of the balanced snow, that is, hc = h - hb where h is the height of the obstruction above the roof surface. 5.4 Drift surcharges The deck is governed by local drift surcharge over much of the roof, so the method is stated here in full and is to be applied exactly as written. 5.4.1 Drift height. For an upwind fetch lu in feet,

[P3] DC2-2026-014  DC-2 Helena Data Centre - Building A EOR-DC-RD-01 Rev 2  -  31 July 2026 Sandalwood Marlow Structural Engineers, PLLC  -  structural design criteria, roof Page 3 hd = 0.43 lu^(1/3) (pg + 10)^(1/4) - 1.5 (ft) with hd taken as zero if the expression is negative. A fetch shorter than 20 ft is taken as lu = 20 ft; there is no upper limit on lu other than the roof itself. 5.4.2 Surcharge shape. A drift forming against an obstruction of clear height hc = h - hb is triangular, with its peak at the face of the obstruction and falling linearly to zero at the far edge of the drift. Where hd is not greater than hc the drift is full height: the peak surcharge is hd x gamma and the drift width is w = 4 hd. Where hd exceeds hc the drift is truncated by the obstruction: the peak surcharge is hc x gamma and the width is w = min(4 hd^2 / hc, 8 hc). The surcharge is added to the balanced load pf, and the balanced load acts over the whole roof including beneath the drift. 5.4.3 Windward face. On the face that the wind arrives at, a windward drift of height 0.75 hd is taken, with lu equal to the roof fetch from the upwind roof edge to that face. 5.4.4 Sheltered face. On the sheltered face, a leeward drift of height hd is taken, with lu equal to the along-wind length of the obstruction itself, that is, the dimension of the obstruction measured in the direction the wind is blowing. The roof of the obstruction is the snow source for that drift. 5.4.5 Wind directions. Wind is considered from each of the four directions in turn. Every obstruction forms a windward drift on the face the wind arrives at and a leeward drift on its sheltered face in each direction. The design surcharge at a point on the roof is the largest of the surcharges produced at that point by the four directions; the four directions are not superimposed. 5.4.6 Parapets. A parapet is treated by the windward rule of clause 5.4.3: the drift height is 0.75 hd with lu equal to the roof dimension upwind of the parapet, and the clear height is hc = parapet height above the roof surface minus hb. The parapet on this project is 3 ft-6 in high on all four sides. 5.4.7 Application to the deck. The deck is a local element. Each deck zone must carry the peak surcharge occurring anywhere within the area it serves, not the average over that area and not the value at its centre. Where a drift crosses a zone boundary the higher demand governs the whole of the zone it falls in. 5.5 Snow buildup at rooftop obstructions Per UFC 3-301-01 paragraph 3-4.1, which adopts ASCE 7-22 Section 7.4 [Supplement], snow buildup around rooftop obstructions is to be considered. Rooftop equipment, equipment curbs, equipment enclosures and screen walls are obstructions. An obstruction standing more than 2.0 ft above the balanced snow surface (that is, hc greater than 2.0 ft) is treated as a drift obstruction and is given the full treatment of clause 5.4 on every face. Shorter obstructions need not be given a drift surcharge, but the balanced load is carried across them. 5.5.1 The equipment enclosure, the equipment screen wall and the packaged rooftop units shown on the current revision of the rooftop equipment plan and in the roof structure model are all obstructions within the meaning of this clause. Their plan position and height are to be taken from the current revision of those documents. 6 Wind loads 6.1 Basic wind speed and velocity pressure. The basic wind speed for the site at the Risk Category III mean recurrence interval is V = 115 mph (3-second gust). The surface roughness at the site is open country and the building is classified Exposure C. The mean roof height is h = 32 ft-0 in. opening frames modelled as axial members around them. The shear that would have passed through an opening
redistributes around it and raises the shear in the deck at the opening corners; that increase is a result of the
analysis, not an assumption.

actually selected, not at an assumed value.

with the capacity of Table 6-1.

Owner's Basis of Design - Excerpt
Document OBD-DC2-A, Revision A. Extract of Sections 1, 3, 5 and 9 issued to the design and construction team for the roof structure package.
1  Project identification
3  Facility description
The building is a single-storey, single-occupancy data centre of 240 ft by 180 ft on plan, framed in structural steel, with the top of roof steel at elevation 32 ft-0 in above finished floor and a continuous 3 ft-6 in parapet on all four sides. The facility supports a designated emergency operations tenant and is therefore classified Risk Category III; the Owner requires that the classification be carried through every load case, including the roof snow and lateral cases, and that it not be traded away in value engineering.
A louvred equipment enclosure and a row of packaged rooftop units stand on the main roof within a screened yard. The roof structure runs continuously beneath the enclosure; the enclosure is not a separate roof level.
3.4  Roof framing and roof deck
The roof framing is open-web steel joists at 6 ft-0 in on centre spanning 30 ft-0 in between joist girders on the transverse column lines. The joist girders are supported on the perimeter columns and on the interior column lines.
The roof deck is to be 1.5 in wide-rib (Type B) steel deck of 3 ft-0 in cover width, spanning across the joists in continuous lengths of not less than three spans wherever the framing allows. Deck gage, support attachment and sidelap connection are to be developed by the structural engineer of record and are to be shown on the roof deck drawing as zones, so that the erector can set out the work without reference to a calculation package.
5  Programme and procurement
The roof structure package is on the critical path. The Owner's procurement strategy assumes that roof-deck material is on site and available to the erector within 9 weeks of release for fabrication. A deck product, gage or finish that cannot meet that allowance is not available to this project, whatever its structural merit, and the design is to be developed accordingly.
Release for fabrication of the roof deck package: on approval of the roof deck drawing and the deck attachment schedule.
Material on site: not later than 9 weeks after that release.
Substitutions that lengthen the delivery are to be raised with the Owner before they are carried into the design, not after.

The following have been agreed with the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) in the pre-application review and are recorded here so that they are not re-opened:
Thermal effects are excluded from the roof deck design. The roof assembly is fully insulated above the deck and the building is conditioned continuously; the AHJ has agreed that self-straining thermal forces need not be combined with the gravity, snow, wind or seismic effects in the design of the roof deck and its attachments.
The ground snow load for the site is established by a site-specific case study rather than by the mapped value. The study is a separate document and is the only source of the ground snow load for this project.
Roof drainage is by internal drains with secondary overflow scuppers through the parapet; ponding instability is addressed by the drainage design and by the deck stiffness requirements of the structural design criteria.

5 Methodology
The study follows the Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory (CRREL) methodology for
site-specific ground snow loads, as used to develop the mapped values in the national standard and as applied in
the published CRREL state and regional snow load studies. The steps are:
5.1 Assemble the annual maximum ground snow water equivalent at each station over its period of record,
converting measured depth to water equivalent where water equivalent was not observed, using the station's own
measured seasonal density where available.
5.2 Fit a log-normal distribution to each station's annual maxima by the method of moments, and extract the
50-year mean recurrence interval value. The log-normal fit is adopted in preference to the Gumbel fit on the
evidence of the probability plots for the valley stations, which show the characteristic upward curvature of a mixed
rain-on-snow population.

water equivalent.

5.5 Check the regression value against the two nearest long-record stations after adjusting them to the site
elevation individually, and against the state study value for the same elevation band. Adopt the regression value
where the checks agree within the standard error, as they do here.
5.6 The analysis period is the 45 water years 1981 to 2025 for the regression stations with concurrent record,
extended to the full period of record at each station for the distribution fitting of paragraph 5.2. No trend adjustment

drift is truncated by the obstruction: the peak surcharge is hc x gamma and the width is w = min(4 hd^2 / hc, 8 hc).
The surcharge is added to the balanced load pf, and the balanced load acts over the whole roof including beneath
the drift.
5.4.3 Windward face. On the face that the wind arrives at, a windward drift of height 0.75 hd is taken, with lu
equal to the roof fetch from the upwind roof edge to that face.
5.4.4 Sheltered face. On the sheltered face, a leeward drift of height hd is taken, with lu equal to the along-wind
length of the obstruction itself, that is, the dimension of the obstruction measured in the direction the wind is
blowing. The roof of the obstruction is the snow source for that drift.
5.4.5 Wind directions. Wind is considered from each of the four directions in turn. Every obstruction forms a
windward drift on the face the wind arrives at and a leeward drift on its sheltered face in each direction. The design
surcharge at a point on the roof is the largest of the surcharges produced at that point by the four directions; the
four directions are not superimposed.
5.4.6 Parapets. A parapet is treated by the windward rule of clause 5.4.3: the drift height is 0.75 hd with lu equal to
the roof dimension upwind of the parapet, and the clear height is hc = parapet height above the roof surface minus
hb. The parapet on this project is 3 ft-6 in high on all four sides.
5.4.7 Application to the deck. The deck is a local element. Each deck zone must carry the peak surcharge
occurring anywhere within the area it serves, not the average over that area and not the value at its centre.
Where a drift crosses a zone boundary the higher demand governs the whole of the zone it falls in.
5.5 Snow buildup at rooftop obstructions
Per UFC 3-301-01 paragraph 3-4.1, which adopts ASCE 7-22 Section 7.4 [Supplement], snow buildup around
rooftop obstructions is to be considered. Rooftop equipment, equipment curbs, equipment enclosures and screen
walls are obstructions. An obstruction standing more than 2.0 ft above the balanced snow surface (that is, hc
greater than 2.0 ft) is treated as a drift obstruction and is given the full treatment of clause 5.4 on every face.
Shorter obstructions need not be given a drift surcharge, but the balanced load is carried across them.
5.5.1 The equipment enclosure, the equipment screen wall and the packaged rooftop units shown on the current
revision of the rooftop equipment plan and in the roof structure model are all obstructions within the meaning of this
clause. Their plan position and height are to be taken from the current revision of those documents.

- Thermal effects are excluded from the roof deck design (roof assembly is fully insulated above the deck and building is conditioned continuously; AHJ agreed self-straining thermal forces need not be combined with gravity, snow, wind or seismic effects).
- Roof framing (open-web steel joists at 6 ft-0 in o.c. spanning 30 ft between joist girders over 240 ft x 180 ft footprint) is fixed and not to be changed.
- Ponding instability is addressed by drainage design (internal drains with secondary overflow scuppers) and by deck stiffness requirements of the structural design criteria.
